title: Seese’s conjecture
formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
definitions: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), membership \(x\in X\) in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class \(C, Sat_{MSO_{1}}(C)\) consists of all finite encoded MSO\(_{1}\) sentences \(\varphi\) for which some \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\). Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory \(Th_{MSO_{1}}(C)\)={\(\varphi\): every \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\)}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in \([k]\), disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The conclusion is \(\exists k\forall G\in C \operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\), with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.

progress.text: Seese establishes foundational connections between decidable monadic graph theories and bounded structural width, and formulates the conjectural MSO\(_{1}\) boundary.
Courcelle–Oum prove that decidable MSO\(_{1}\) with parity predicates implies bounded clique-width.
Dawar–Sankaran develop the antichain/minimal-hereditary-class reduction for the stronger grid-interpretation conjecture; preprint 2020, CSL 2022, journal volume 2025.
Mählmann characterizes bounded shrub-depth through logical expressiveness and records a stronger MSO-dependence conjecture that would imply Seese’s.
Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk prove bounded clique-width for hereditary 2-WQO classes; the hypothesis differs from decidability of MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO\(_{1}\) decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.

context_blocks.text: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO\(_{1}\) conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether \(n\in S\) if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO\(_{1}\) with the predicate \(Even(X)\), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO\(_{1}\) sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO\(_{1}\) formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO\(_{1}\) decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.

sentences: MSO1 permits quantification over vertices and vertex sets in a graph.
Seese's conjecture asks whether decidability of this logic over a graph class forces bounded clique-width.
The proposed implication connects an algorithmic property of the class's whole logical theory with a finite construction complexity for its graphs.
A proof would identify a strong structural obstruction to decidable graph reasoning.

The saved formulation imposes no hereditary assumption and excludes edge-set and counting extensions, so results for narrower classes or stronger logics cannot be substituted for the stated general MSO1 question.
